vignette:
He is 25, a Latin American man who works as a data scientist, and when he tells the story it always begins with his younger sister at seven years old, lying in a hospital bed with wires on her chest and an oxygen mask too large for her face. He is fifteen then, old enough to understand the fear in the adults around him but too young to do anything useful with it. Before that week, his life feels ordinary in memory-school, crowded dinners, teasing his sister over homework, his mother calling both of them to the table. Then she develops a high fever that does not break, and within days the family is told she might not survive the infection.

He remembers the hospital in fragments that still feel sharper than yesterday: the chemical smell of sanitizer, the sound of rubber soles on the floor at night, his father standing with both hands on his head as if trying to hold himself together. He sits in plastic chairs for hours, watching nurses move quickly in and out of the room. Sometimes he is sent home, but he cannot really leave. Even from his bed he imagines monitors failing, imagines her lungs stopping, imagines his mother alone in the room when it happens. He keeps his phone in his hand and stares at it until dawn. When it lights up, his stomach drops before he can even read the message.

His sister survives, but the danger does not end cleanly. There are complications, follow-up visits, another brief hospitalization, months of uncertainty. The family speaks of gratitude, of miracles, of being strong. He tries to do the same. At school he says she is "better now" and shrugs when friends ask questions. Inside, he feels as if something has been left switched on. He starts checking on her at night, standing in her doorway to see if her chest is moving. If she coughs, he is instantly awake. If his mother's voice changes even slightly on the phone, heat rushes through him.

By late adolescence he becomes the dependable one. He learns to excel quietly, to keep his mind occupied. Numbers begin to feel safer than people. In college he gravitates toward statistics and programming because the logic is soothing: inputs, models, outputs, patterns that can be understood if he works hard enough. He does well enough to build a career as a data scientist, and from the outside his life looks stable. He has an apartment, a good job, a reputation for being calm under pressure. Coworkers know him as precise and thoughtful, the one who catches anomalies no one else sees.

But his mind is still organized around catastrophe. In meetings, if someone says a project is "critical," his body reacts before his thoughts do-heart racing, shoulders tightening, a sudden sense that something irreversible is about to happen. He keeps multiple monitors open and checks dashboards compulsively, refreshing data pipelines long after he knows they are running normally. He tells himself he is being thorough. In quieter moments he recognizes the feeling from the hospital: the belief that if he watches closely enough, he might prevent disaster.

He avoids certain things without fully admitting that he is avoiding them. He does not visit friends in hospitals after surgeries; he sends food, apologizes, says work is busy. Medical dramas on television make him leave the room. He has trouble when his family posts photos of his sister from that time on anniversaries, calling it the year they "fought together." He cannot look for long. Sometimes, late at night, an image comes back with no warning-his sister's hand limp against the blanket, a doctor using the word "unstable," his mother crying in a bathroom because she thinks no one can hear. When that happens, he feels pulled out of the present. He closes his laptop and paces the apartment, checking his phone for messages from home even when there is no reason to expect bad news.

Sleep is uneven. He falls asleep with ease only when exhausted, and even then he wakes at small sounds. If his sister, now healthy and living independently, does not answer a text, he cycles quickly from mild concern to certainty that something terrible has happened. He knows this reaction is out of proportion, and that awareness makes him feel ashamed rather than relieved. He does not tell many people how much of his attention is still tethered to her survival.

Relationships are difficult in a way he struggles to explain. He wants closeness but feels most comfortable when he is the one anticipating someone else's needs, scanning for risk, staying a step ahead. Dating has been brief and unsatisfying. When partners ask for emotional openness, he becomes distant or overly analytical, as if he can convert feeling into information and thereby make it manageable. Under stress he grows irritable, especially when others seem careless about health or safety. Then he feels guilty for being harsh.

Now, at 25, he speaks about the experience with a kind of controlled fluency, as though he has rehearsed it into something coherent. But the emotional logic of his life still bends around that hospital room. He moves through the world as if loss is always one missed sign away, as if vigilance is the price of love, and as if relaxing his guard-even for a moment-might invite the worst thing back.
